title: The history of the rainbow
tagline: From a Greek idea of mirrors in the clouds to light bending inside a single raindrop, and the maths that finally got every faint arc right.
intro: People have asked what a rainbow is for more than two thousand years. The big clue was that one drop of water can bend light, bounce it, and bend it again. Thinkers in Greece, Egypt, Iran, Germany, England and France each added a piece. Some pieces were lost for centuries, and some were found twice. Here is how the puzzle came together.

eras.name: Mirrors in the clouds
eras.summary: Greek writers think the rainbow is a reflection in a cloud. In Cairo, Ibn al-Haytham builds the optics that later work needs. In China, Sun Sikong and Shen Kuo say sunlight meets rain.

eras.name: One drop at a time
eras.summary: Roger Bacon measures the bow. Al-Shirazi, al-Farisi and Theodoric use water-filled glass globes as giant raindrops. They find the path of light inside a drop.

eras.name: Law and colour
eras.summary: Harriot, Snell and Descartes find the sine law of refraction. Descartes uses it to work out the bow's angle. Newton shows that white light holds every colour.

eras.name: Light as a wave
eras.summary: Young uses interference to explain the faint extra bows. Airy builds a wave theory of the rainbow.

eras.name: The full theory
eras.summary: Mie's exact maths for light on a sphere covers the whole rainbow. Nussenzveig's work shows why Airy's curve sits inside it. Students still repeat the old flask experiment.

events.title: Aristotle says the rainbow is a reflection
events.text: In his Meteorology, Aristotle says the rainbow is sight reflected off tiny water drops in a cloud, back toward the sun. He says it never makes more than a semicircle, that it is lower when the sun is higher, and that there are at most two bows at once.
events.why: It was the first serious study of the rainbow, and it set the question for the next 1,600 years.

events.title: Aristotle notes rainbows made by the moon
events.text: Aristotle writes that moon rainbows are rare. They need a full moon, near rising or setting. He says he had seen only two in more than fifty years. Their colours were hard to see, so they looked almost white.
events.why: It is an early record of the moonbow, which is the same bow cast by a much dimmer light.

events.title: Seneca weighs the theories
events.text: In Natural Questions, Seneca sets out several ideas about the rainbow. He favours one in which the sun reflects off a cloud shaped like a curved mirror.
events.why: Roman writers kept the cloud-mirror idea alive.

events.title: The dark band between two rainbows
events.text: Alexander of Aphrodisias, writing on Aristotle's Meteorology, was the first to describe the dark patch of sky between a primary and a secondary bow. It is still called Alexander's band. Raindrops cannot send light to the eye from that region.
events.why: The dark band is a clue that something in the drop caps the angle of the light.

events.title: The Book of Optics
events.text: Ibn al-Haytham wrote the seven-volume Kitab al-Manazir. It covers light, sight and refraction, and it describes testing ideas with experiments. He tried a water-filled globe, but he did not link it to the raindrop. He thought a rainbow was an image in the cloud, like a curved mirror.
events.why: Al-Farisi and Theodoric built their rainbow theories on this book.

events.title: Sunlight meets rain
events.text: In the Dream Pool Essays, Shen Kuo says a rainbow forms when sunlight shines on rain. He credits an earlier scholar, Sun Sikong (1015-1076), with the idea.
events.why: It names rain and sun as the cause, without a cloud mirror.

events.title: Bacon measures the bow
events.text: In the Opus Majus, Roger Bacon reports that the top of the rainbow cannot rise above about 42 degrees over the horizon. He probably used an astrolabe. He also stressed the role of single water drops.
events.why: The rainbow now had a number that any theory had to match.

events.title: Al-Shirazi turns to drops
events.text: Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi (1236-1311) taught al-Farisi and sent him to read Ibn al-Haytham. Some scholars credit him with the first correct rainbow theory. Roshdi Rashed argues against that.
events.why: A teacher's question started the work that solved the rainbow.

events.title: A water globe as a giant raindrop
events.text: In De iride, Theodoric used a glass globe full of water as a magnified raindrop in a dark room. Light is refracted going in, reflects once inside, and is refracted coming out. He saw that a second bow comes from two reflections, which flips its colours.
events.why: It explains both bows from what happens inside one drop.

events.title: Al-Farisi tests a sphere in a dark chamber
events.text: Al-Farisi finished the Tanqih al-Manazir in Ramadan 708 AH, which is early 1309. He put a large glass sphere of water in a camera obscura. He argued that light is refracted twice in a drop, with one or more reflections between. MacTutor calls it the first mathematically satisfactory explanation. He seems to have worked without any contact with Theodoric.
events.why: The same answer was found twice, in Iran and in Germany, at about the same time.

events.title: Harriot finds the sine law
events.text: Harriot discovered the sine law of refraction in July 1601. He did not publish it. By 1606 he was working on a theory of the rainbow, and he published none of that either.
events.why: Without the law of refraction, nobody could calculate the bow.

events.title: Snell finds the law again
events.text: Snell found the law of refraction in 1621 but never published it. It became known when Huygens printed it in 1703.
events.why: It is why the law is called Snell's law in many countries.

events.title: Descartes calculates the rainbow
events.text: Descartes published Les Meteores with his Discourse on Method. He used the law of refraction, a refractive index of 4/3 for water, and the geometry of a round drop. The primary bow comes from one internal reflection and the secondary from two. He got both angles right, but not the colours.
events.why: It turned a long-argued idea into a number that anyone could check.

events.title: Sunlight is a mix of colours
events.text: Newton sent the Royal Society a paper arguing that sunlight is a mixture of rays that bend by different amounts. Colour belongs to the rays, not to the glass. Added to Descartes' theory, this explains why a rainbow spreads into a band, with red bent the least.
events.why: It explains why one drop makes a spectrum.

events.title: Opticks
events.text: Newton delayed Opticks until after his rival Robert Hooke died in 1703. It covers the colours of thin films and the diffraction of light. Newton first named five main colours and later seven.
events.why: It became the standard book on light and colour for a century.

events.title: Young explains the extra bows
events.text: Young read his lecture on interference to the Royal Society in November 1803. He used it to explain supernumerary bows, the faint extra arcs just inside the main one. Newton's particle idea of light could not do that.
events.why: The faint bows showed that light behaves like a wave.

events.title: Airy's wave theory of the rainbow
events.text: Airy was then Astronomer Royal. In a paper on the light near a caustic, he used wave theory to show that the rainbow's brightness is finite and not infinite. His theory also gives the faint extra bows. Drop size matters, and very small drops give a wide, pale bow.
events.why: It explained the bow's fine detail, including the white fogbow.

events.title: Lorenz solves light on a sphere
events.text: The Danish physicist Ludvig Lorenz worked out how a plane light wave scatters from a transparent sphere. Mie reached the same theory independently. It is now sometimes called Lorenz-Mie theory.
events.why: An exact answer for a round drop was available years before Mie.

events.title: Mie's exact theory
events.text: Mie published exact equations for how light scatters from a sphere in the Annalen der Physik. Physics World says the theory gives a complete theory of the rainbow, though the sums are very slow to work out for raindrops.
events.why: Maxwell's equations for light could now be solved for a raindrop.

events.title: Nussenzveig finds Airy inside Mie
events.text: Michael Berry writes that Nussenzveig extended Mie's work in the 1960s and found the Airy integral inside it. This linked the exact theory to the older wave picture.
events.why: It showed that the old and new theories agree.

events.title: The theory of the rainbow, for everyone
events.text: Nussenzveig wrote The Theory of the Rainbow for Scientific American. It says the answer needs all the resources of mathematical physics.
events.why: It gave the public a map of the whole theory.

events.title: The flask experiment, tested again
events.text: Two Leipzig physicists studied the round-bottom flask rainbow experiment. They note that such experiments go back to Theodoric in the 14th century and Descartes. They confirm the 42 degree bow in a flask.
events.why: A 700-year-old classroom experiment still holds up.

series.title: The rainbow's angle, as measured or calculated
series.caption: The number stays close to 42 degrees from Bacon's time to ours.

points.label: Bacon: top of the bow is about 42 degrees up
Selmke and Selmke: 42 degrees for a flask
Modern theory: red light, about 42.5 degrees

series.title: The bending power of water
series.caption: Descartes used 4/3. Modern values for red and blue differ slightly, which is why the bow spreads into colours.

facts: Descartes used a refractive index of 4/3 for water, and it gave the right angle.
Aristotle said he had seen only two moon rainbows in more than fifty years.
Al-Farisi and Theodoric seem to have solved the rainbow separately, at about the same time.
The dark band between two bows is named for Alexander of Aphrodisias.
Fogbows look white because their droplets are under 0.05 mm across.
